did_you_know.text: Did you know? The opening verse identifies the work as "The Song of Songs" and attributes it to Solomon.
Did you know? In the song, the beloved’s name is compared to oil poured out—that is, fragrant oil whose scent spreads; therefore the young women love him.
Did you know? The woman describes herself as "black and beautiful" and compares the appearance of her tents to the tents of Kedar and the curtains of Solomon.
Did you know? The woman explains that her dark complexion was caused by exposure to the sun, and says that her mother’s sons made her tend the vineyards—even though she did not tend her own vineyard.
Did you know? The woman asks where her beloved grazes his flock at noon, so that she will not have to be like one who covers herself or wanders beside the flocks of his companions.
Did you know? The beloved compares the woman to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots, an image that emphasizes her beauty, splendor, and impressive presence in his eyes.
Did you know? The beloved promises the woman jewelry described as gold ornaments decorated with silver studs, as part of his praise of her beauty.
Did you know? While the king is at his banquet, the woman’s nard is described as giving off its fragrance; nard is an aromatic substance that also appears in the song’s descriptions of perfumes.
Did you know? The beloved is also compared to a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En Gedi, bringing both a natural landscape and a real place known for its desert oasis into the song.
Did you know? The song ends with a description of a shared home whose beams are cedars and whose rafters are firs—a picture of a stable, pleasant, and refreshing space.
